17       This case comes before the Court on Defendant’s motion to dismiss.  Plaintiff filed 
18  an opposition to the motion, and Defendant filed a reply.  For the reasons set out below, 
19  the motion is denied.                                                     
20                                    I.                                      
21                              BACKGROUND                                    
22        Plaintiff  Biological  Dynamics  is  a  “leader  in  exosome  isolation  technology.”  
23  (Compl. ¶ 2.)  According to the Complaint,                                
24       [e]xosomes and other extracellular vesicles are nonparticles secreted by all 
        cell  types  into  the  blood  or  other  biofluids.    These  nanoparticles  carry 
25                                                                            
        biomarkers of the cell from which they originated.  Isolating exosomes and 
26       extracellular vesicles allows researchers and professionals to then test for such 
        biomarkers  to  determine  disease  characteristics  and  propensities.    As 
27                                                                            
        exosomes exist at an early stage of any disease, technology that can isolate 
28       and test exosomes allows for the ‘holy grail’ – enabling early detection of 
1       diseases (such as cancer) long before symptoms appear and at a time when 
        treatment can be most effective.                                     
2                                                                            

3  (Id.)  “A critical part of Biological Dynamics’ overall technology is its isolation platform—
4  sometimes referred to as a ‘lab-on-a-chip’ platform.”  (Id. ¶ 3.)  This platform “utilizes a 
5  proprietary  semiconductor  chip  that  works  in  connection  with  Biological  Dynamics’ 
6  proprietary instruments, hardware, and software to isolate exosomes with minimum pre-
7  processing, thereby preserving biomolecules that would otherwise be lost in alternative 
8  approaches.”  (Id.)  Biological Dynamics developed this platform “over more than a decade 
9  and at immense expense[,]” and it “protects its investment and intellectual property through 
10  both trade secrets and a large patent portfolio.”  (Id. ¶ 4.)             
11       Those trade secrets are the subject of this case.  (Id.)  Specifically, Plaintiff alleges 
12  that  two  of  its  former  VP-level  employees,  Richard  Young  and  Bryan  Rice, 
13  misappropriated Plaintiff’s trade secrets after they were terminated from their employment 
14  with  Plaintiff.    Armed  with  those  trade  secrets,  Young  and  Rice  formed  Defendant 
15  Exokeryx,  which  has  “virtually  replicated  Biological  Dynamics’  business  by  cloning 
16  Biological Dynamics’ proprietary ‘lab-on-a-chip’ platform and core technology.”  (Id. ¶ 
17  6.)                                                                       
18       Plaintiff  alleges  Defendant  operated  in  “stealth”  mode  from  its  formation  in 
19  November 2021 until November 2022, and when it “exited ‘stealth’ mode” it “provided 
20  data on experiments that it had run, indicated that it had already filed patent applications, 
21  and announced that it would launch its first product ‘ExoPrep,’ in 2023.”  (Id. ¶ 7.)  Plaintiff 
22  alleges Defendant                                                         
23       simply could not have developed such complicated technology, nor advanced 
        its  business,  that  quickly  without  the  use  of  Biological  Dynamics’  trade 
24                                                                            
        secrets,  including  Biological  Dynamics’  proprietary  processes  and 
25       technologies.  Others in this field indicate that the average time to market is 
        over 15 years—a time horizon confirmed by the fact that it took Biological 
26                                                                            
        Dynamics and its preeminent engineers and executives over a decade to 
27       advance its development to its current commercial status.            

28                                                                            
1  (Id.)                                                                     
2       To confirm its suspicions about Exokeryx, Plaintiff ran a forensic analysis of the 
3  laptop that had been previously issued to and used by Rice during his employment with 
4  Plaintiff.  (Id. ¶ 8.)  That analysis revealed that after Rice was terminated, “he connected a 
5  USB ‘thumb’ drive to” the laptop, and “[b]etween 9 p.m. until after midnight, Rice 
6  proceeded to copy critical Biological Dynamics’ documents onto it.  Then, on the day Rice 
7  agreed to appear at Biological Dynamics’ offices to surrender his Company laptop, Rice 
8  spent the morning permanently deleting thousands of files from it.”  (Id.)   
9       After finding this information, Plaintiff sent a letter to Young and Rice reminding 
10  them of their contractual obligations to maintain the confidentiality of Plaintiff’s trade 
11  secrets and other proprietary information and to return any company-issued property.  (Id. 
12  ¶ 45.)  When Plaintiff did not receive a satisfactory response to its letter, it filed an 
13  arbitration demand against Young and Rice to enforce their contractual obligations under 
14  their employment-related agreements.  (Id.)  During the arbitration proceedings, Young 
15  and  Rice  challenged  certain  provisions  of  their  employment-related  contracts  as 
16  unenforceable restraints under California Business and Professions Code Section 16600.  
17  (Id. ¶ 45 n.1.)  The arbitrator ruled in favor of Young and Rice, and invalidated the 
18  challenged provisions on nondisclosure and nonuse.  (Id.)                 
19       On August 25, 2023, Rice and Young filed a petition to confirm the arbitrator’s 
20  decision in San Diego Superior Court.1  Approximately two weeks after Rice and Young 
21  filed that petition, Plaintiff filed the present case against Exokeryx alleging claims for 
22  misappropriation of trade secrets under the Defend Trade Secrets Act  (“DTSA”) and 
23  California’s  Uniform  Trade  Secrets  Act (“CUTSA”).    In  response  to  the  Complaint, 
24  Defendant filed the present motion.                                       
25  / / /                                                                     
26                                                                            

27                                                                            
   1 The state court recently issued an order confirming the arbitrator’s decision.  (See Supp. 
28                                                                            
1                                    II.                                     
2                               DISCUSSION                                   
3       Defendant moves to dismiss this case on two grounds.  First, it argues the arbitration 
4  decision and the state court order confirming that decision render this case res judicata.  
5  Second, Defendant asserts Plaintiff has failed to allege sufficient facts to support the 
6  element of misappropriation.                                              
7  A.   Res Judicata                                                         
8       An affirmative defense, such as res judicata, may be raised in a motion to dismiss 
9  under Rule 12(b)(6) only when “the defense raises no disputed issues of fact,” Scott v. 
10  Kuhlmann, 746 F.2d 1377, 1378 (9th Cir. 1984), and the affirmative defense “clearly 
11  appears on the face of” the complaint.  Boquist v. Courtney, 32 F.4th 764, 774 (9th Cir. 
12  2022).  On the first requirement, Defendant’s res judicata argument relies on the Complaint 
13  in this case, Plaintiff’s complaints in arbitration, and the arbitrator’s final decision, all of 
14  which are the proper subject of judicial notice.2  Defendant’s reliance on these documents 
15  does not raise any disputed issues of fact, therefore the first requirement is met.  The second 
16  requirement is also met because the arbitration proceeding clearly appears on the face of 
17  the Complaint.  (Compl. ¶ 45.)                                            
18                                                                            

19                                                                            
   2 A court may consider “matters of judicial notice” in ruling on a motion to dismiss.  United 
20                                                                            
   States v. Ritchie, 342 F.3d 903, 908 (9th Cir. 2003).  Here, Defendant asked the Court to 
21  take judicial notice of the arbitration documents mentioned above and eight additional 
   documents,  including  Rice  and  Young’s  petition  to  confirm  the  arbitration  award, 
22                                                                            
   Plaintiff’s petition to vacate the arbitration award, discovery requests from the arbitration 
23  proceedings, and Plaintiff’s Employee Handbook.  (See Request for Judicial Notice in 
   Supp. of Mot. (“RJN”), ECF No. 9-1.)  Plaintiff filed a response to Defendant’s Request 
24                                                                            
   for Judicial Notice in which it argued that although the Court could take judicial notice of 
25  the fact of these documents, it could not take judicial notice of the documents’ contents.  
   In its reply brief, Defendant clarified that, other than the allegations in the arbitration 
26                                                                            
   complaints, it is not requesting that the Court take judicial notice of the contents of any of 
27  these documents.  With that clarification, the Court grants Defendant’s request to take 
   judicial notice of the allegations in the arbitration complaints and the arbitrator’s final 
28                                                                            
1       Those initial requirements being satisfied, the Court now turns to consider whether 
2  federal or state law applies to the parties’ res judicata dispute.  Defendant urges the Court 
3  to apply federal law while Plaintiff contends that California law applies.  Ninth Circuit case 
4  law supports Plaintiff’s position.  See Caldeira v. Cnty. of Kauai, 866 F.2d 1175, 1178 (9th 
5  Cir. 1989) (applying Hawaii law to question of preclusive effect of arbitration award 
6  reviewed by Hawaii state court).  Thus, the Court will apply California law.   
7       Under California law:                                                
8       [r]es judicata applies if (1) the decision in the prior proceeding [was] final and 
        on the merits; (2) the present proceeding is on the same cause of action as the 
9                                                                            
        prior proceeding; and (3) the parties in the present proceeding or parties in 
10       privity with them were parties to the prior proceeding.              
11  Rangel v. PLS Check Cashers of California, Inc., 899 F.3d 1106, 1110 (9th Cir. 2018) 
12  (quoting Fed'n of Hillside & Canyon Ass'ns v. City of Los Angeles, 126 Cal. App. 4th 1180, 
13  1202 (2004)).  As the party asserting this defense, Defendant bears the burden to show each 
14  of these requirements is met.  Patel v. Crown Diamonds, Inc., 247 Cal. App. 4th 29, 40 
15  (2016) (quoting Vella v. Hudgins, 20 Cal. 3d 251, 257 (1977)).            
16       1.   Final Decision on the Merits                                    
17       To meet its burden on the first requirement, Defendant relies on the arbitrator’s 
18  decision.  In its opposition to the motion, Plaintiff argued that decision was not final 
19  because the petitions to confirm and vacate the decision were still pending in state court.  
20  Since that time, the state court has issued its decision confirming the arbitrator’s decision, 
21  (see Supp. RJN, Exs. K, L), which defeats Plaintiff’s argument.  Plaintiff also argued the 
22  arbitrator’s decision would not be final until all appeals from the state court decision were 
23  resolved.  At this time, however, there is no evidence before the Court that Plaintiff has 
24  filed an appeal.  Unless or until such an appeal is filed, the arbitrator’s decision is final.   
25       The next issue is whether the arbitrator’s decision was “on the merits.”  “A judgment 
26  is on the merits for purposes of res judicata ‘if the substance of the claim is tried and 
27  determined.’”  Ass’n of Irritated Residents v. Dept. of Conservation, 11 Cal. App. 5th 1202, 
28  1220 (2017) (quoting Johnson v. City of Loma Linda, 24 Cal. 4th 61, 77 (2000)) (quotation 
1  marks omitted).  Here, the arbitrator found “the pertinent clauses [of the contracts in 
2  question] are illegal, and in violation of the public policy as stated in Business and 
3  Professions Code section 16600.”  (RJN, Ex. C at 128.3)  Defendant argues that finding is 
4  a decision on the merits.  Plaintiff does not necessarily disagree with that argument.  
5  Instead, it argues the arbitrator’s decision did not reach the merits of the claims asserted in 
6  this case.  But that is not the question here.  The question here is whether the arbitrator 
7  rendered a decision on the merits of the claims in arbitration.  On that question, the Court 
8  agrees with Defendant that the arbitrator’s decision was “on the merits.”  Accordingly, 
9  Defendant has met its burden on the first element of res judicata.        
10       2.   Same Cause of Action                                            
11       In an effort to meet its burden on the second element, Defendant relies on what it 
12  calls the “same transactional nucleus of facts” test.  Rather than being a freestanding test, 
13  whether two actions arise out of the “same transactional nucleus of facts” is but one factor 
14  federal courts consider in determining whether there is an “identity of claims” for the 
15  purpose of res judicata.  Turtle Island Restoration Network v. United States Dept. of State, 
16  673 F.3d 914, 917-18 (9th Cir. 2012) (setting out four factors for determining whether there 
17  is an “identity of claims” for res judicata).                             
18       Regardless, this test does not apply here.  Instead, “California courts employ the 
19  ‘primary rights’ theory to determine what constitutes the same cause of action for claim 
20  preclusion purposes[.]”  Maldonado v. Harris, 370 F.3d 945, 952 (9th Cir. 2004).   
21       The primary right theory is a theory of code pleading that has long been 
        followed in California.  It provides that a “cause of action” is comprised of a 
22                                                                            
        “primary  right”  of  the  plaintiff,  a  corresponding  “primary  duty”  of  the 
23       defendant, and a wrongful act by the defendant constituting a breach of that 
        duty.  The most salient characteristic of a primary right is that it is indivisible:  
24                                                                            
        the violation of a single primary right gives rise to but a single cause of action.   
25                                                                            
26                                                                            

27                                                                            
   3 The page number cited here and all further citations to the RJN correspond to the page 
28                                                                            
1  Crowley v. Katleman, 8 Cal. 4  666, 681 (1994) (citations omitted).  Under the primary 
2  rights theory, a cause of action “is the right to obtain redress for a harm suffered, regardless 
3  of the specific remedy sought or the legal theory (common law or statutory) advanced.”  
4  Boeken v. Philip Morris USA, Inc., 48 Cal. 4th 788, 797 (2010).  As stated in Boeken, “under 
5  the primary rights theory, the determinative factor is the harm suffered.  When two actions 
6  involving the same parties seek compensation for the same harm, they generally involve 
7  the same primary right.”  Id. at 798 (citing Agarwal v. Johnson, 25 Cal. 3d 932, 954 (1979)).   
8       Although Defendant did not address the primary rights theory in its opening brief, 
9  in its reply brief Defendant argues the harm alleged in the arbitration proceeding is the 
10  same  harm  alleged  in  the  present  case,  namely  Defendant’s  unfair  competition  with 
11  Plaintiff.  (Reply at 6.)  However, that is an oversimplification of the pleadings and the 
12  harm alleged in the arbitration proceeding.  There, Plaintiff alleged harms in the form of 
13  loss of control over its proprietary information, loss of its employees, and loss of severance 
14  payments made to Rice and Young.  (RJN, Ex. A at 16, 19.)  In the present case, Plaintiff 
15  alleges loss of control over its trade secrets and unfair competition on the part of Defendant.  
16  Although  the  arbitration  claims  may  reference  Defendant’s  unfair  competition  with 
17  Plaintiff, it bears mention that neither Rice nor Young, on their own, could have engaged 
18  in unfair competition with Plaintiff.  That specific form of harm, e.g., harm to Plaintiff’s 
19  “competitive position  in  the  market,”  and  “missed  fundraising  opportunities  and  lost 
20  sales[,]” (Compl. ¶ 71), could only have occurred through the actions of Defendant, which 
21  was under no contractual obligation to Plaintiff and therefore did not participate in the 
22  arbitration.  That Plaintiff referenced Defendant’s unfair competition in the claims for 
23  arbitration does not mean that harm was in issue.  Accordingly, the Court finds the second 
24  requirement for res judicata is not met.4                                 
25  / / /                                                                     
26                                                                            

27                                                                            
   4 Although  this  finding  resolves  the  issue  of  whether  res  judicata  applies,  the Court 
28                                                                            
1       3.   Privity                                                         
2       To satisfy the third requirement of privity, Defendant again relies on federal law, but 
3  in its reply Defendant states privity also exists under California law.  To establish privity 
4  under California law, Defendant must show that it “shared ‘an identity or community of 
5  interest, with adequate representation of that interest in the first suit, and circumstances 
6  such that the nonparty should reasonably have expected to be bound by the first suit.’”  
7  Grande v. Eisenhower Med. Ctr., 13 Cal. 5th 313, 326 (2022) (quoting DKN Holdings LLC 
8  v. Faerber, 61 Cal.4th 813, 826 (2015) (internal quotation marks omitted).   
9       Starting with the third element, Defendant argues it is met here because Plaintiff 
10  alleged in the arbitration proceedings that Defendant would be bound by the results of that 
11  proceeding.  (Reply at 3-4.)  However, nowhere in the statement of claim did Plaintiff so 
12  allege.    As  stated  above,  Plaintiff  certainly  mentioned  Defendant  in  the  arbitration 
13  proceedings, but the mere mention of Defendant does not amount to an allegation that 
14  Defendant would be bound by the results of those proceedings.  Even if Plaintiff did so 
15  allege, that allegation would not constitute an admission or evidence that Defendant either 
16  reasonably expected or otherwise agreed to be bound by the arbitrator’s decision.   
17       On the contrary, given that the arbitration proceedings were based on contracts 
18  between Plaintiff and Rice and Young only, the more plausible conclusion is Defendant 
19  would not have reasonably expected to be bound by the arbitration proceedings.  Rice and 
20  Young having prevailed in those proceedings makes it convenient for Defendant to now 
21  suggest that it expected to be bound by the arbitrator’s decision.  But it strains credulity to 
22  think Defendant would be taking that same position had the arbitrator ruled in favor of 
23  Plaintiff.  On the record currently before the Court, Defendant has not shown the third 
24  element of privity is satisfied.  For this reason, and in light of Defendant’s failure to show 
25  that the harm alleged in this case is the same harm at issue in the arbitration, the Court 
26  denies Defendant’s motion to dismiss this case as res judicata.           
27  / / /                                                                     
28  / / /                                                                     
1  B.   Failure to State a Claim                                             
2       The only other basis for Defendant’s motion is Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 
3  12(b)(6).  To survive a motion to dismiss under this Rule, “a complaint must contain 
4  sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its 
5  face.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal, 556 U.S. 662, 678 (2009) (citing Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 
6  550 U.S. 544, 570 (2007)).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
7  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
8  for the misconduct alleged.”  Id. (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556).      
9       “Determining whether a complaint states a plausible claim for relief will ... be a 
10  context-specific task that requires the reviewing court to draw on its judicial experience 
11  and common sense.”  Id. at 679 (citing Iqbal v. Hasty, 490 F.3d 143, 157-58 (2d Cir. 2007)).  
12  In Iqbal, the Court began this task “by identifying the allegations in the complaint that are 
13  not  entitled  to  the  assumption  of  truth.”    Id.  at  680.  It  then  considered  “the  factual 
14  allegations in respondent’s complaint to determine if they plausibly suggest an entitlement 
15  to relief.”  Id. at 681.                                                  
16       Here, Plaintiff’s claims both allege trade secret misappropriation, one claim arising 
17  under the DTSA and the other arising under the CUTSA.  “To succeed on a claim for 
18  misappropriation of trade secrets under the DTSA, a plaintiff must prove: (1) that the 
19  plaintiff possessed a trade secret, (2) that the defendant misappropriated the trade secret; 
20  and (3) that the misappropriation caused or threatened damage to the plaintiff.”  Inteliclear, 
21  LLC v. ETC Global Holdings, Inc., 978 F.3d 653, 657-58 (9th Cir. 2020).  The elements 
22  under CUTSA are similar.  See Sargent Fletcher, Inc. v. Able Corp., 110 Cal. App. 4th 
23  1658, 1665-66 (2003) (citations omitted) (stating elements of CUTSA claim are: “(1) the 
24  plaintiff owned a trade secret, (2) the defendant acquired, disclosed, or used the plaintiff’s 
25  trade  secret  through  improper  means,  and  (3)  the  defendant’s  actions  damaged  the 
26  plaintiff.”)                                                              
27       In the motion, Defendant argues Plaintiff has failed to allege sufficient facts to 
28  support the misappropriation element.  Under the DTSA, misappropriation is defined as: 
1       (A) acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has 
        reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or  
2                                                                            

3       (B) disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied 
        consent by a person who –                                            
4                                                                            

5       (i) used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret;    

6                                                                            
        (ii) at the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that the 
7       knowledge of the trade secret was—                                   

8                                                                            
        (I) derived from or through a person who had used improper means to acquire 
9       the trade secret;                                                    

10                                                                            
        (II) acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain the secrecy 
11       of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or         

12                                                                            
        (III) derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking 
13       relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade 
        secret; or                                                           
14                                                                            

15       (iii) before a material change of the position of the person, knew or had reason 
        to know that –                                                       
16                                                                            

17       (I) the trade secret was a trade secret; and                         

18                                                                            
        (II) knowledge of the trade secret had been acquired by accident or mistake[.]   
19                                                                            
20  18 U.S.C. § 1839(5).  See also Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1(b) (setting out nearly identical 
21  definition of misappropriation).                                          
22       Contrary to Defendant’s argument, Plaintiff has alleged sufficient facts to support 
23  this element.  For instance, Plaintiff alleges that in the two months prior to being terminated 
24  from the Company, Rice “downloaded and copied” confidential documents containing 
25  Plaintiff’s trade secrets, including Plaintiff’s “Blue Book.”  (Compl. ¶ 51.)  Plaintiff notes 
26  that Rice “had not accessed that Blue Book in the full year prior” to his termination.  (Id.)  
27  Plaintiff further alleges that after his termination, Rice “installed and used an external USB 
28  ‘thumb’ drive … to access and copy Company files[,]” (id. ¶ 53), including files “labeled 
1  ‘Confidential’ on the face of the documents,” and files with “Confidential” in the filename.  
2  (Id. ¶ 54.)  Plaintiff further alleges that prior to returning his Company laptop, Rice 
3  “attempted to permanently delete thousands of [Plaintiff’s] documents from his Company 
4  laptop.”  (Id. ¶ 57.)  In addition, after Plaintiff discovered Rice’s use of the thumb drive 
5  and confronted Rice about it, Rice claimed “he ‘disposed’ of it and other hard copy files 
6  related to his work with the Company that he kept after his termination.”  (Id. ¶ 58.) 
7       Plaintiff then alleges that less than six months after Rice and Young were terminated 
8  from the Company, they founded Exokeryx, the Defendant in this case.  (Id. ¶ 61.)  Plaintiff 
9  alleges Defendant                                                         
10       knew that its founders, Rice and Young, had no right to copy, take or use 
        [Plaintiff’s] trade secrets.  Given Rice and Young are founders and officers of 
11                                                                            
        Exokeryx, Defendant cannot deny that it knew of the contractual obligations 
12       and the terms of the Employee Handbook and Code of Business Conduct and 
        Ethics Policy—obligations that Rice and Young … agreed to in order to 
13                                                                            
        protect [Plaintiff’s] trade secrets.                                 
14                                                                            
15  (Id. ¶ 76.)  Plaintiff further alleges that despite Defendant’s alleged knowledge of Rice and 
16  Young’s  misappropriation,  Defendant  then  hired  several  more  of  Plaintiff’s  former 
17  employees.  (Id. ¶ 6.)  A year after Rice and Young founded Exokeryx, it “provided data 
18  on experiments that it had run, indicated it had already filed patent applications, and 
19  announced that it would launch its first product, ‘ExoPrep,’ in 2023.”  (Id. ¶ 7.)  Plaintiff 
20  alleges Defendant’s website now “contains a three-part product roadmap” that “tracks 
21  exactly the three generations of products at Biological Dynamics.”  (Id. ¶ 47.)   
22       Defendant takes these and other allegations from the Complaint, isolates them, and 
23  argues that each specific allegation is insufficient to allege misappropriation.  However, 
24  that approach ignores the broader context in which the alleged facts took place, which the 
25  Court  must  consider  in  deciding  the  present  motion.    See  Iqbal,  556  U.S.  at  679 
26  (“Determining whether a complaint states a plausible claim for relief will, …, be a context-
27  specific task that requires the reviewing court to draw on its judicial experience and 
28  common sense.”)  Defendant also draws inferences from the allegations in its favor, which 
1   |/is inconsistent with the standard applicable to motions to dismiss.  Under the appropriate 
2   ||standard, the Court finds Plaintiff has  alleged sufficient “factual content that allows the 
3   ||court  to  draw  the  reasonable  inference  that  the  defendant  is  liable  for  the  misconduct 
4   |lalleged.”  Jd. at 678 (citing Twombly, 550 U.S. at 556).  Accordingly, Defendant’s motion 
5   ||to dismiss the claim under Rule 12(b)(6) is denied. 
6                                           III. 
7                              CONCLUSION AND ORDER 
8         For the reasons set out above, Defendants’ motion to dismiss is denied. 
9         IT IS SO ORDERED.

3       Defendant moves to dismiss this case on two grounds.  First, it argues the arbitration 
4  decision and the state court order confirming that decision render this case res judicata.  
5  Second, Defendant asserts Plaintiff has failed to allege sufficient facts to support the

7  A.   Res Judicata                                                         
8       An affirmative defense, such as res judicata, may be raised in a motion to dismiss 
9  under Rule 12(b)(6) only when “the defense raises no disputed issues of fact,” Scott v. 
10  Kuhlmann,
746 F.2d 1377, 1378
 (9th Cir. 1984), and the affirmative defense “clearly 
11  appears on the face of” the complaint.  Boquist v. Courtney,
32 F.4th 764
, 774 (9th Cir. 
12  2022).  On the first requirement, Defendant’s res judicata argument relies on the Complaint 
13  in this case, Plaintiff’s complaints in arbitration, and the arbitrator’s final decision, all of 
14  which are the proper subject of judicial notice.2  Defendant’s reliance on these documents 
15  does not raise any disputed issues of fact, therefore the first requirement is met.  The second 
16  requirement is also met because the arbitration proceeding clearly appears on the face of 
17  the Complaint.  (Compl. ¶ 45.)

1       Those initial requirements being satisfied, the Court now turns to consider whether 
2  federal or state law applies to the parties’ res judicata dispute.  Defendant urges the Court 
3  to apply federal law while Plaintiff contends that California law applies.  Ninth Circuit case 
4  law supports Plaintiff’s position.  See Caldeira v. Cnty. of Kauai,
866 F.2d 1175, 1178
 (9th 
5  Cir. 1989) (applying Hawaii law to question of preclusive effect of arbitration award 
6  reviewed by Hawaii state court).  Thus, the Court will apply California law.   
7       Under California law:                                                
8       [r]es judicata applies if (1) the decision in the prior proceeding [was] final and 
        on the merits; (2) the present proceeding is on the same cause of action as the 
9                                                                            
        prior proceeding; and (3) the parties in the present proceeding or parties in 
10       privity with them were parties to the prior proceeding.              
11  Rangel v. PLS Check Cashers of California, Inc.,
899 F.3d 1106, 1110
 (9th Cir. 2018) 
12  (quoting Fed'n of Hillside & Canyon Ass'ns v. City of Los Angeles,
126 Cal. App. 4th 1180
, 
13  1202 (2004)).  As the party asserting this defense, Defendant bears the burden to show each 
14  of these requirements is met.  Patel v. Crown Diamonds, Inc.,
247 Cal. App. 4th 29
, 40 
15  (2016) (quoting Vella v. Hudgins,
20 Cal. 3d 251, 257
 (1977)).            
16       1.   Final Decision on the Merits                                    
17       To meet its burden on the first requirement, Defendant relies on the arbitrator’s 
18  decision.  In its opposition to the motion, Plaintiff argued that decision was not final 
19  because the petitions to confirm and vacate the decision were still pending in state court.  
20  Since that time, the state court has issued its decision confirming the arbitrator’s decision, 
21  (see Supp. RJN, Exs. K, L), which defeats Plaintiff’s argument.  Plaintiff also argued the 
22  arbitrator’s decision would not be final until all appeals from the state court decision were 
23  resolved.  At this time, however, there is no evidence before the Court that Plaintiff has 
24  filed an appeal.  Unless or until such an appeal is filed, the arbitrator’s decision is final.   
25       The next issue is whether the arbitrator’s decision was “on the merits.”  “A judgment 
26  is on the merits for purposes of res judicata ‘if the substance of the claim is tried and 
27  determined.’”  Ass’n of Irritated Residents v. Dept. of Conservation,
11 Cal. App. 5th 1202
, 
28  1220 (2017) (quoting Johnson v. City of Loma Linda,
24 Cal. 4th 61, 77
 (2000)) (quotation 
1  marks omitted).  Here, the arbitrator found “the pertinent clauses [of the contracts in 
2  question] are illegal, and in violation of the public policy as stated in Business and 
3  Professions Code section 16600.”  (RJN, Ex. C at 128.3)  Defendant argues that finding is 
4  a decision on the merits.  Plaintiff does not necessarily disagree with that argument.  
5  Instead, it argues the arbitrator’s decision did not reach the merits of the claims asserted in 
6  this case.  But that is not the question here.  The question here is whether the arbitrator 
7  rendered a decision on the merits of the claims in arbitration.  On that question, the Court 
8  agrees with Defendant that the arbitrator’s decision was “on the merits.”  Accordingly, 
9  Defendant has met its burden on the first element of res judicata.        
10       2.   Same Cause of Action                                            
11       In an effort to meet its burden on the second element, Defendant relies on what it 
12  calls the “same transactional nucleus of facts” test.  Rather than being a freestanding test, 
13  whether two actions arise out of the “same transactional nucleus of facts” is but one factor 
14  federal courts consider in determining whether there is an “identity of claims” for the 
15  purpose of res judicata.  Turtle Island Restoration Network v. United States Dept. of State, 
16
673 F.3d 914, 917-18
 (9th Cir. 2012) (setting out four factors for determining whether there 
17  is an “identity of claims” for res judicata).                             
18       Regardless, this test does not apply here.  Instead, “California courts employ the 
19  ‘primary rights’ theory to determine what constitutes the same cause of action for claim 
20  preclusion purposes[.]”  Maldonado v. Harris,
370 F.3d 945, 952
 (9th Cir. 2004).   
21       The primary right theory is a theory of code pleading that has long been 
        followed in California.  It provides that a “cause of action” is comprised of a 
22                                                                            
        “primary  right”  of  the  plaintiff,  a  corresponding  “primary  duty”  of  the 
23       defendant, and a wrongful act by the defendant constituting a breach of that 
        duty.  The most salient characteristic of a primary right is that it is indivisible:  
24                                                                            
        the violation of a single primary right gives rise to but a single cause of action.   
25

1  Crowley v. Katleman,
8 Cal. 4
  666, 681 (1994) (citations omitted).  Under the primary 
2  rights theory, a cause of action “is the right to obtain redress for a harm suffered, regardless 
3  of the specific remedy sought or the legal theory (common law or statutory) advanced.”  
4  Boeken v. Philip Morris USA, Inc.,
48 Cal. 4th 788, 797
 (2010).  As stated in Boeken, “under 
5  the primary rights theory, the determinative factor is the harm suffered.  When two actions 
6  involving the same parties seek compensation for the same harm, they generally involve 
7  the same primary right.”
Id.
 at 798 (citing Agarwal v. Johnson,
25 Cal. 3d 932, 954
 (1979)).   
8       Although Defendant did not address the primary rights theory in its opening brief, 
9  in its reply brief Defendant argues the harm alleged in the arbitration proceeding is the 
10  same  harm  alleged  in  the  present  case,  namely  Defendant’s  unfair  competition  with 
11  Plaintiff.  (Reply at 6.)  However, that is an oversimplification of the pleadings and the 
12  harm alleged in the arbitration proceeding.  There, Plaintiff alleged harms in the form of 
13  loss of control over its proprietary information, loss of its employees, and loss of severance 
14  payments made to Rice and Young.  (RJN, Ex. A at 16, 19.)  In the present case, Plaintiff 
15  alleges loss of control over its trade secrets and unfair competition on the part of Defendant.  
16  Although  the  arbitration  claims  may  reference  Defendant’s  unfair  competition  with 
17  Plaintiff, it bears mention that neither Rice nor Young, on their own, could have engaged 
18  in unfair competition with Plaintiff.  That specific form of harm, e.g., harm to Plaintiff’s 
19  “competitive position  in  the  market,”  and  “missed  fundraising  opportunities  and  lost 
20  sales[,]” (Compl. ¶ 71), could only have occurred through the actions of Defendant, which 
21  was under no contractual obligation to Plaintiff and therefore did not participate in the 
22  arbitration.  That Plaintiff referenced Defendant’s unfair competition in the claims for 
23  arbitration does not mean that harm was in issue.  Accordingly, the Court finds the second 
24  requirement for res judicata is not met.4

1       3.   Privity                                                         
2       To satisfy the third requirement of privity, Defendant again relies on federal law, but 
3  in its reply Defendant states privity also exists under California law.  To establish privity 
4  under California law, Defendant must show that it “shared ‘an identity or community of 
5  interest, with adequate representation of that interest in the first suit, and circumstances 
6  such that the nonparty should reasonably have expected to be bound by the first suit.’”  
7  Grande v. Eisenhower Med. Ctr.,
13 Cal. 5th 313
, 326 (2022) (quoting DKN Holdings LLC 
8  v. Faerber,
61 Cal.4th 813, 826
 (2015) (internal quotation marks omitted).   
9       Starting with the third element, Defendant argues it is met here because Plaintiff 
10  alleged in the arbitration proceedings that Defendant would be bound by the results of that 
11  proceeding.  (Reply at 3-4.)  However, nowhere in the statement of claim did Plaintiff so 
12  allege.    As  stated  above,  Plaintiff  certainly  mentioned  Defendant  in  the  arbitration 
13  proceedings, but the mere mention of Defendant does not amount to an allegation that 
14  Defendant would be bound by the results of those proceedings.  Even if Plaintiff did so 
15  allege, that allegation would not constitute an admission or evidence that Defendant either 
16  reasonably expected or otherwise agreed to be bound by the arbitrator’s decision.   
17       On the contrary, given that the arbitration proceedings were based on contracts 
18  between Plaintiff and Rice and Young only, the more plausible conclusion is Defendant 
19  would not have reasonably expected to be bound by the arbitration proceedings.  Rice and 
20  Young having prevailed in those proceedings makes it convenient for Defendant to now 
21  suggest that it expected to be bound by the arbitrator’s decision.  But it strains credulity to 
22  think Defendant would be taking that same position had the arbitrator ruled in favor of 
23  Plaintiff.  On the record currently before the Court, Defendant has not shown the third 
24  element of privity is satisfied.  For this reason, and in light of Defendant’s failure to show 
25  that the harm alleged in this case is the same harm at issue in the arbitration, the Court 
26  denies Defendant’s motion to dismiss this case as res judicata.

1  B.   Failure to State a Claim                                             
2       The only other basis for Defendant’s motion is Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 
3  12(b)(6).  To survive a motion to dismiss under this Rule, “a complaint must contain 
4  sufficient factual matter, accepted as true, to ‘state a claim to relief that is plausible on its 
5  face.’”  Ashcroft v. Iqbal,
556 U.S. 662, 678
 (2009) (citing Bell Atlantic Corp. v. Twombly, 
6
550 U.S. 544, 570
 (2007)).  “A claim has facial plausibility when the plaintiff pleads factual 
7  content that allows the court to draw the reasonable inference that the defendant is liable 
8  for the misconduct alleged.”
Id.
 (citing Twombly,
550 U.S. at 556
).      
9       “Determining whether a complaint states a plausible claim for relief will ... be a 
10  context-specific task that requires the reviewing court to draw on its judicial experience 
11  and common sense.”
Id.
 at 679 (citing Iqbal v. Hasty,
490 F.3d 143, 157-58
 (2d Cir. 2007)).  
12  In Iqbal, the Court began this task “by identifying the allegations in the complaint that are 
13  not  entitled  to  the  assumption  of  truth.”    Id.  at  680.  It  then  considered  “the  factual 
14  allegations in respondent’s complaint to determine if they plausibly suggest an entitlement 
15  to relief.”  Id. at 681.                                                  
16       Here, Plaintiff’s claims both allege trade secret misappropriation, one claim arising 
17  under the DTSA and the other arising under the CUTSA.  “To succeed on a claim for 
18  misappropriation of trade secrets under the DTSA, a plaintiff must prove: (1) that the 
19  plaintiff possessed a trade secret, (2) that the defendant misappropriated the trade secret; 
20  and (3) that the misappropriation caused or threatened damage to the plaintiff.”  Inteliclear, 
21  LLC v. ETC Global Holdings, Inc.,
978 F.3d 653, 657-58
 (9th Cir. 2020).  The elements 
22  under CUTSA are similar.  See Sargent Fletcher, Inc. v. Able Corp.,
110 Cal. App. 4th 23 1658, 1665-66
 (2003) (citations omitted) (stating elements of CUTSA claim are: “(1) the 
24  plaintiff owned a trade secret, (2) the defendant acquired, disclosed, or used the plaintiff’s 
25  trade  secret  through  improper  means,  and  (3)  the  defendant’s  actions  damaged  the 
26  plaintiff.”)                                                              
27       In the motion, Defendant argues Plaintiff has failed to allege sufficient facts to 
28  support the misappropriation element.  Under the DTSA, misappropriation is defined as: 
1       (A) acquisition of a trade secret of another by a person who knows or has 
        reason to know that the trade secret was acquired by improper means; or  
2                                                                            

3       (B) disclosure or use of a trade secret of another without express or implied 
        consent by a person who –                                            
4                                                                            

5       (i) used improper means to acquire knowledge of the trade secret;    

6                                                                            
        (ii) at the time of disclosure or use, knew or had reason to know that the 
7       knowledge of the trade secret was—                                   

8                                                                            
        (I) derived from or through a person who had used improper means to acquire 
9       the trade secret;                                                    

10                                                                            
        (II) acquired under circumstances giving rise to a duty to maintain the secrecy 
11       of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade secret; or         

12                                                                            
        (III) derived from or through a person who owed a duty to the person seeking 
13       relief to maintain the secrecy of the trade secret or limit the use of the trade 
        secret; or                                                           
14                                                                            

15       (iii) before a material change of the position of the person, knew or had reason 
        to know that –                                                       
16                                                                            

17       (I) the trade secret was a trade secret; and                         

18                                                                            
        (II) knowledge of the trade secret had been acquired by accident or mistake[.]

20
18 U.S.C. § 1839
(5).  See also
Cal. Civ. Code § 3426.1
(b) (setting out nearly identical

        Exokeryx, Defendant cannot deny that it knew of the contractual obligations

556 U.S. at 679
 
26  (“Determining whether a complaint states a plausible claim for relief will, …, be a context-
